data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

When something starts, stops, speeds up, slows down, or turns, look for an unbalanced push or pull. A moving object does not always need an ongoing unbalanced force.

1. Read **The Invisible Push**.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Look at the **Push, Pull, Stop** chart.
4. Sort the cards in **Balanced or Unbalanced?**
5. Practise explaining with **Force Detective Frames**, then check yourself against the rubric.
6. Take the quiz. Question 3 is about a ball that rolls and stops.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Invisible Push** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Investigation: The Ramp Race** — change one thing, and write down your guess first.

This week, observe a change in motion and explain what push or pull may have caused it. 🛼

history.title: The Invisible Push
history.meta: 3rd Grade • Leveled reading • forces, motion, and evidence
history.data:
## The Invisible Push

Roll a ball across the floor. It travels, slows, and stops. Nobody touches it with a hand, but the floor is touching it all along. The air around it matters too.

A **force** is a push or a pull. Forces can change motion: starting, stopping, speeding up, slowing down, or turning. A force can also act without making an object move. Press gently on a wall: you apply a push even if the wall stays still.

When you kick a ball, your foot pushes it while they touch. After your foot leaves, the ball can keep moving. It does not carry a continuing push from your foot.

**Friction** acts between touching surfaces and resists sliding between them. It can help your shoes grip the ground. Contact with the floor can also resist a ball's rolling, especially when the ball or surface bends a little. Air resistance can slow motion too. A ball often rolls farther on a firm smooth floor than on thick carpet, but compare the same ball and release to test your surfaces.

**Gravity** pulls objects toward Earth. A dropped pencil falls because of that pull. Gravity also acts on a book resting on a table. The table pushes upward on the book.

If all the forces on one object cancel overall, they are **balanced**. A still book stays still. An object already moving keeps the same speed in a straight line while its forces remain balanced. Balanced does not mean no forces.

If the forces do not cancel overall, they are **unbalanced** and the object's motion changes. A toy cart can speed up, slow down, or turn. The direction it is moving is not always the direction of the overall force: a force against its motion can slow it down.

A bicycle can move steadily while you pedal. On a straight, level path, the forward effect of pedaling can balance the forces resisting motion. A larger forward force makes it speed up. A turning bicycle changes direction even if its speed stays the same.

Careful observations reveal **patterns**. Release the same ball from the same place on a ramp without an extra push. Repeat the test and mark where it stops. The marks may be close together rather than identical. Use that pattern to **predict** an approximate stopping place for another roll. Then test your prediction and report what you actually observe.

data.title: Remember the Invisible Push
data.instructions: Two cards lock in the big ideas from The Invisible Push. Look at the example, make your own, and tell how it helps you remember.
data.sourceExcerpt: Friction resists sliding between surfaces. Gravity pulls nearby objects toward Earth. Balanced forces keep speed and direction unchanged; unbalanced forces change motion.

essentialFacts: Friction resists sliding between touching surfaces and helps shoes grip.
Contact with the floor can resist rolling; compare surfaces using the same ball and release.
Gravity pulls nearby objects toward Earth, including objects sitting still.
cards.aiExample: FRICTION: feel the grip of a shoe. GRAVITY: think of a dropped pencil going toward the ground.
cards.mapping: The shoe reminds you that friction can provide grip as well as resist sliding. The pencil reminds you of gravity.
coachPrompts: Which of your two hooks explains the ball on the carpet?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own sound or word hooks for the two forces.
cards.reasoningPrompt: Tell how each hook helps you remember what that force does.

hookFact.text: Gravity is always pulling on you, even right now while you sit still.

cards.target: Balanced forces keep motion the same; unbalanced forces change it
essentialFacts: Balanced forces on one object cancel overall.
Balanced forces allow rest or constant speed in a straight line.
Unbalanced forces change speed or direction.
cards.aiExample: A still book stays still when its forces balance. A moving cart keeps steady straight-line motion when its forces balance. Unequal horizontal forces change the cart motion.
cards.mapping: Track a single object. Balance means unchanged motion, not necessarily no motion.
cards.scaffoldStarter: A still object with balanced forces ____. A moving object with balanced forces ____.
scaffoldSteps: Explain what happens when its forces stop balancing.
coachPrompts: Can your model show a moving object with balanced forces?
cards.studentPrompt: Draw or describe your own balanced-and-unbalanced picture.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture show when motion changes?

hookFact.text: The chair is pushing up on you exactly as hard as gravity is pulling down. That is why you are not falling.

history.title: Force Detective Frames
history.meta: 6 frames • say them out loud before writing • rubric included

items.text: The ____ started to move because of a ____ (push or pull) from ____.
The rolling ball slowed down. Contact with the ____ and resistance from the ____ can explain this.
With the same ball and release, our ball rolled ____ on ____. I think this happened because ____.
When I let go of the ____, ____ pulled it toward the ground.
The forces on the ____ were ____ (balanced or unbalanced), and I know because it ____.
I predict that if I ____, the ____ will ____, because ____.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Force Detective |
|---|---|---|---|
| Naming the force | Says something moved | Names a push or a pull | Names the push or pull AND what it came from |
| Force words | Everyday words only | Uses 1-2 glossary words correctly | Uses 3+ glossary words correctly, including friction or gravity |
| Predicting | Guesses with no reason | Predicts and gives a reason | Predicts, gives a reason from the reading, and says how to test it |

questions.question: Which answer gives the general meaning of a force?
options: A push or a pull
Anything that is moving
A kind of energy in batteries
The weight of an object

questions.question: You drop a pencil and it falls to the floor. Which force pulled it down?
options: Friction
Gravity
Magnetism
Wind

questions.question: A ball rolls across a floor and slowly stops without another hand touching it. Which explanation fits?
options: The ball ran out of energy and got tired
Gravity pulled it backward
Contact with the floor and resistance from the air can slow it
Balls always stop after a few seconds
questions.correctAnswer: Contact with the floor and resistance from the air can slow it

questions.question: Two equal opposite horizontal pulls act on a rope that remains still. How do these horizontal forces compare?
options: Unbalanced, because both teams are pulling hard
There are no forces, because nothing is moving
Balanced, because the pulls are equal and opposite
Gravity, because the rope is heavy
questions.correctAnswer: Balanced, because the pulls are equal and opposite

questions.question: You roll a ball down a ramp three times from the same spot, and it stops near the same place each time. What can you do with that pattern?
options: Nothing, because every roll is different
Prove that friction does not exist on ramps
Make the ball roll forever by trying again
Predict about where it will stop on the fourth roll
questions.correctAnswer: Predict about where it will stop on the fourth roll

questions.question: A book stays still on a table. Gravity pulls it down. Explain why it does not fall, using the word balanced.
questions.expectedAnswer: The table pushes up on the book and gravity pulls down. These forces act on the same book and balance, so its motion does not change.

questions.question: In our test, the same ball released the same way rolled farther on a firm floor than on carpet. Explain a possible reason using friction or resistance.
questions.expectedAnswer: The carpet may resist rolling more in this setup as the ball and surface deform. Contact effects, including friction, and air resistance can slow motion. Repeated controlled rolls help check the comparison.

reflections.text: Name a change in motion you observed. What force might explain it?
Where in your home is there a lot of friction? Where is there very little?

data.question: Can a bike keep moving while its forces are balanced?
data.answer: Yes. At steady speed in a straight line, the forward effect of pedaling balances forces resisting motion. A larger forward force makes it speed up. Coasting usually lets resistance slow it down.

data.question: Why does ice make you slip?
data.answer: Shoes need friction to grip the ground. A slippery surface can provide less grip, so the shoe slides. Friction does not only slow things down: it also helps you walk.

data.question: Does gravity work on the Moon? 🌙
data.answer: Yes. Gravity near the Moon surface is weaker than near Earth surface. Gravity depends on mass and distance, not simply on how big something looks.

data.question: Can a force happen without touching?
data.answer: Yes! Gravity pulls the pencil without touching it. A magnet can pull a paperclip across a gap. Most pushes and pulls you do use touching. Not all forces do.

data.question: If I push a wall and it does not move, did I use a force? 🧱
data.answer: Yes. Your hand pushes on the wall, and the wall pushes back on your hand. Those two forces act on different objects. The wall stays still because your push is balanced by other forces on the wall, including support from the building.

data.question: Why do heavy things not fall faster?
data.answer: When air resistance is negligible, objects fall with the same acceleration near Earth regardless of their mass. In air, shape, size, and mass affect how much air resistance changes the fall. Compare carefully rather than assuming all balls land together.

history.title: Investigation: The Ramp Race
history.meta: 3rd Grade • Investigation brief • one ramp, one change, a prediction

data.title: The Ramp Race
data.instructions: Roll a ball down a ramp, measure how far it goes, and change one thing to see what happens. Guess first, then test, then use your pattern to predict a roll you have not done yet.
data.fitReason: The standard asks third graders to observe motion, find a pattern, and predict. A ramp with one change at a time makes friction and unbalanced forces something they measure with a tape.

brief.context: Your class has a board for a ramp, some books to prop it up, a tennis ball, and a measuring tape. There are three floors to try: tile, carpet, and a rubber mat.
brief.audience: Your class, and the class next door who will try to beat your prediction
brief.drivingQuestion: When we change one thing about the ramp or the floor, how does the distance the ball rolls change? Can we predict a roll before we make it?
brief.seedDirection: Change only the ramp height OR the floor surface. Use the same ball and ramp. Release from the same marked place without an extra push. Repeat three times for each setup and measure from the ramp bottom to the stopping place.
lockedLessonFacts: A force is a push or a pull; forces can balance even when an object is moving.
Contact with the floor can resist rolling. Surface effects vary, so compare them with a controlled test.
Gravity pulls the ball toward Earth; on the ramp this can make it roll downhill.
Repeated observations can support an approximate prediction, not a guaranteed result.
openQuestions: Which surface produces the shortest rolling distance in our controlled setup?
How does raising the ramp affect the distances we measure?
How many rolls do we need before we trust our pattern?
stakeholders: The teacher who lends the books
criteria: Only one thing changes between setups
Three rolls for every setup, measured with the tape and written in a table
A written guess before each new setup
A prediction for a setup you have not tried, made from the pattern. Then a test of it.
Uses the words friction and predict correctly
constraints: Ramp no taller than three books
Everyone stays out of the ball's path
brief.deliverable: A data table (setup, roll 1, roll 2, roll 3). Your guesses. Your prediction for the setup you did not try, and how close it was. And two sentences about what friction did.

parallelExample.context: A class compared a toy car on a firm floor and a rug.
parallelExample.move: They used the same car and ramp, released from the same place without pushing, repeated each setup, and measured each stopping distance. They used the spread of results to predict another trial.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: They changed only the surface and checked how consistent their results were. A prediction can be useful without being exact.

supports.frameStarter: We changed ____. We think the ball will go ____ because ____. It went ____.
frameChoices: Change the floor surface while keeping the ramp fixed
Change ramp height while keeping the same floor and ball
Predict the next roll in a setup already measured
coachPrompts: Did you change only one thing? Say what stayed the same.
Which surface gave the shortest distance? What other conditions might also affect the result?
What is your guess for the next roll, and what pattern gave you that guess?

data.coachHint: One change, repeated measurements, then a prediction. Record variation and unexpected results too.
data.sourceExcerpt: Release from the same place without an extra push. Repeat the test, compare the stopping places, and use the pattern to predict an approximate result.
